rootQuestion: Are there infinitely many primes of the form n^2 + 1?

workingPaperSections.body:
Research workstream: Small examples and counterexamples

Computation:
- Command: python3 search.py
- Exit code: 0

Findings:
- Computation checked exactly: \[ 1 \le n \le 200,\qquad n^2+1 \le 40001. \]
- Run data:
- command exited with code \(0\),
- runtime: \(104\) ms,
- no stderr output. Finite result: \[ 34 \] values of \(n\) in the range produced primes \(n^2+1\). Prime-producing examples include: \[ \begin{aligned} &1,2,4,6,10,14,16,20,24,26,36,40,54,56,66,74,84,90,94,\\ &110,116,120,124,126,130,134,146,150,156,160,170,176,180,184. \end{aligned} \] Theorem-level local facts:
- If \(n>1\) is odd, then \(n^2+1\) is even and greater than \(2\), hence composite.
- Therefore only \(n=1\) and even \(n\) are eligible for primality.
- In the range \(1\le n\le 200\), there are \(101\) eligible values: \(n=1\) plus \(100\) even \(n\).
- Among eligible values, the observed finite prime rate was \[ \frac{34}{101}\approx 0.337. \] For an odd prime \(p\mid n^2+1\), one has \[ n^2\equiv -1 \pmod p, \] so \(-1\) is a quadratic residue modulo \(p\). Hence necessarily \[ p\equiv 1 \pmod 4. \] This matches the observed small divisors \(5,13,17,29,37,41,\dots\). Observed congruence obstructions included: \[ \begin{array}{c|c} p & r \text{ with } p\mid r^2+1\\ \hline 5 & 2,3\\ 13 & 5,8\\ 17 & 4,13\\ 29 & 12,17\\ 37 & 6,31\\ 41 & 9,32 \end{array} \]

Limitations:
- This finite search is not a proof that infinitely many primes of the form \[ n^2+1 \]
- exist.
- The root question is a famous open problem, related to Landau’s problems. No known argument proves infinitude.
- The observed rate \(34/101\) is descriptive only. It cannot be extrapolated into an asymptotic density or an infinitude theorem.
- Small-divisor patterns explain many composites but do not prevent arbitrarily long composite stretches, nor do they force infinitely many primes.
- A finite computation does not prove an infinite claim.

Open gaps:
- No global mechanism is supplied for producing infinitely many \(n\) such that \(n^2+1\) is prime.
- No sieve bound strong enough to isolate infinitely many primes is established.
- No analytic theorem about the distribution of primes represented by \(n^2+1\) is proved.
- The computation only verifies primality and factorization in the small range \(1\le n\le 200\).

Next: Extend the finite search to larger bounds while clearly separating computation from proof. Record gaps between prime-producing \(n\). Compare observations with the Bateman–Horn heuristic for \(n^2+1\).

Project coordinator synthesis

What we know:
- Finite computation checked exactly \[ 1\le n\le 200,\qquad n^2+1\le 40001. \] It found \(34\) prime-producing \(n\)’s. A skeptic check confirmed no missing or extra reported prime-producing \(n\)’s in that range.
- If \(n\) is odd and \(n>1\), then \[ n^2+1\equiv 2\pmod 4, \] so \(n^2+1\) is composite.
- Thus only \(n=1\) and even \(n\) can produce primes.
- Equivalently, all nontrivial cases reduce to \[ n=2m,\qquad n^2+1=4m^2+1. \]

researchPaths.title: Direct proof attempt
researchPaths.objective: Look for a direct proof strategy or obstruction for Are there infinitely many primes of the form n^2 + 1.
latestFindings: Complete modular obstruction is impossible: for every modulus \(m\), \[ r\equiv 0\pmod m\implies \gcd(r^2+1,m)=1. \]

Finite prime coverings are impossible. For a finite set \(S\) of relevant primes, \[ p=2 \text{ excludes one class},\qquad p\equiv1\pmod4 \text{ excludes two classes}. \] Hence the admissible density is \[ \frac12\prod_{\substack{p\in S\\ p\equiv1(4)}}\left(1-\frac2p\right)>0. \]
Therefore, if all \(n^2+1\) were composite, the responsible prime divisors must vary over an unbounded set.

Positive finite-sieve density may still vanish when the sieve level grows with \(n\).
Existing almost-prime results do not bridge the full gap to primality.

steps.title: Literature findings
details: No supplied source gives an accepted unconditional settlement of infinitely many primes of the one-variable form \(n^2+1\).

The only direct source is a 2017 arXiv preprint claiming/proposing a rigorous spectral-method proof for infinitely many “quadratic twin primes” \(n^2+1,n^2+3\); its own summary frames this as a proposed proof, not established literature consensus [source-5].

A related unconditional-looking theorem claim: Merikoski proves infinitely many primes of the multivariable forms \[ X^2+(Y^2+1)^2,\qquad X^2+(Y^3+Z^3)^2, \] using Harman’s sieve; this does not specialize to infinitely many primes \(n^2+1\) because the theorem allows auxiliary variables to vary [source-2].

The same source reports Friedlander–Iwaniec’s theorem giving an asymptotic for primes of the form \(X^2+Y^4\), again a two-variable representation theorem, not a fixed-fiber theorem with \(Y=1\) [source-2]. **Theorem check**

Carella’s source invokes a “recent heuristic argument” based on spectral analysis and proposes a rigorous version proving infinitely many primes \(n^2+1\) and \(n^2+3\) simultaneously [source-5].
This is direct but should be treated as heuristic/proposed unless independently validated; it must not be upgraded to an unconditional theorem from the supplied metadata alone [source-5].

details: No complete local obstruction was found for moduli \(m\le 5000\): for every tested \(m\), at least one residue class \(r\bmod m\) has \[ \gcd(r^2+1,m)=1. \]
Minimum admissible residue count in this range is \(1\), attained trivially at \(m=2\).
Sample admissible densities: \[ m=4,8,16:\ 1/2,\qquad m=10,20,60,120,840,2520:\ 0.3. \]

Finite covering by prime divisors \(p\le 200\) fails. Relevant primes are \(p=2\) and primes \(p\equiv 1\bmod 4\). The uncovered density modulo their squarefree product is positive, about \[ 0.14126. \]
Extending the finite covering check to relevant primes \(p\le 10000\) still leaves positive uncovered density, about \[ 0.08347. \]

Among \(n\le 200000\), there are \(16572\) values for which \(n^2+1\) has no divisor among relevant primes \(\le 10000\). First examples: \[ 110,116,120,124,126,130,134,146,150,156,\dots \] with corresponding values \[ 12101,13457,14401,15377,15877,16901,17957,21317,22501,24337. \]

For disproving infinitude by a local/covering obstruction, one would need a modulus \(m\) such that every residue class forces a nontrivial common divisor of \(n^2+1\) with \(m\), or a covering by finitely many prime-divisibility classes.
The tested data gives no sign of such an obstruction.

Structurally, only \(p=2\) and primes \(p\equiv 1\bmod 4\) can divide some \(n^2+1\); each odd such prime excludes exactly \(2\) residue classes mod \(p\), leaving proportion \(1-2/p\). Finite products therefore leave a positive proportion of uncovered classes.
The computations rule out only complete obstructions up to \(m\le 5000\) and finite coverings using relevant primes \(\le 10000\).
This does not prove infinitely many primes of the form \(n^2+1\).
It also does not rule out a more subtle global obstruction, e.g. one not expressible as a finite modular covering in the tested range.
Extend complete modulus search beyond \(5000\), though the structural product behavior suggests finite local obstruction is unlikely.
Search instead for stronger negative evidence: long intervals where all \(n^2+1\) are composite, or patterns forcing many small factors.
Separately distinguish primality data from local admissibility data: survivors of small-prime sieving need not be prime.

steps.title: Critic review
steps.summary: Reviewing the attempt for gaps before updating the working paper.
details: The computational “complete local obstruction” search is essentially vacuous: for every modulus \(m\), the residue \(r\equiv 0\pmod m\) gives \[ \gcd(r^2+1,m)=\gcd(1,m)=1. \] Thus no modulus \(m\) can make every residue class share a nontrivial divisor with \(m\). This is a proof, not just evidence up to \(5000\).

The finite-prime covering obstruction can also be ruled out structurally for any finite set of primes: for each relevant odd \(p\equiv1\pmod4\), only two residue classes mod \(p\) are excluded, and for \(p=2\), only one class is excluded. CRT leaves admissible classes.
The admissible-density computations are consistent with local sieving, but they do not materially advance the direct proof attempt.
Local admissibility is only a necessary condition for possible infinitude, not a route to proving primes of the form \(n^2+1\).
Survivors after sieving by primes \(\le 10000\) need not be prime; the listed examples should not be treated as primality evidence unless factored or primality-tested.
The phrase “more subtle global obstruction” is too vague. If all \(n^2+1\) were composite, the obstructing divisors would necessarily vary with \(n\), since finite prime coverings are impossible.
No mechanism is proposed to turn positive finite-sieve survivor density into infinitely many primes.
No standing-constraint violation detected: the attempt does not cite Euclid-style infinitude, generic prime infinitude, heuristic preprints, or multivariable polynomial-prime theorems as proof.
No named theorem is invoked without applicability checks.
The main overstatement is presenting finite searches as meaningful negative evidence against local obstruction when the obstruction is impossible for elementary reasons.

details: The computational “complete local obstruction” search is essentially vacuous: for every modulus \(m\), the residue \(r\equiv 0\pmod m\) gives \[ \gcd(r^2+1,m)=\gcd(1,m)=1. \] Thus no modulus \(m\) can make every residue class share a nontrivial divisor with \(m\). details: Replace finite local-obstruction searches by a moving sieve problem: \[ n^2+1\text{ prime}\iff p\nmid n^2+1\quad\text{for every prime }p\le n. \]
Finite sieves are useful only as diagnostics; a proof needs control as the sieving range grows with \(n\).

literatureSources.title: Infinitely many prime knots with the same Alexander invariants
literatureSources.summary: We revisit the issue of the existence of infinitely many distinct prime knots with the same Alexander invariant. We present infinitely many distinct families, each family made up of infinitely many distinct knots. Within each family, the Alexander invariant is the same. Unlike other examples in the literature, ours are elementary and based on a sub-collection of pretzel knots with three tassels.

literatureSources.title: The polynomials $X^2+(Y^2+1)^2$ and $X^{2} + (Y^3+Z^3)^2$ also capture their primes
literatureSources.summary: We show that there are infinitely many primes of the form $X^2+(Y^2+1)^2$ and $X^2+(Y^3+Z^3)^2$. This extends the work of Friedlander and Iwaniec showing that there are infinitely many primes of the form $X^2+Y^4$. More precisely, Friedlander and Iwaniec obtained an asymptotic formula for the number of primes of this form. For the sequences $X^2+(Y^2+1)^2$ and $X^2+(Y^3+Z^3)^2$ we establish Type II information that is too narrow for an aysmptotic formula, but we can use Harman's sieve method to produce a lower bound of the correct order of magnitude for primes of form $X^2+(Y^2+1)^2$ and $X^2+(Y^3+Z^3)^2$. Estimating the Type II sums is reduced to a counting problem which is solved by using the Weil bound, where the arithmetic input is quite different from the work of Friedlander and Iwaniec for $X^2+Y^4$. We also show that there are infinitely many primes $p=X^2+Y^2$ where $Y$ is represented by an incomplete norm form of degree $k$ with $k-1$ variables. For this we require a Deligne-type bound for correlations of hyper-Kloosterman sums.

literatureSources.title: An elemetary proof of an estimate for a number of primes less than the product of the first $n$ primes
literatureSources.summary: Let $α$ be a real number such that $1< α<2$ and let $x_0=x_0(α)$ be a {\rm(}unique{\rm)} positive solution of the equation $$ x^{α-1} -\fracπ{e^2\sqrt{3}}x +1=0. $$ Then we prove that for each positive integer $n>x_0$ there exist at least $[n^α]$ primes between the $(n+1)$th prime and the product of the first $n+1$ primes. In particular, we establish a recent Cooke's result which asserts that for each positive integer $n$ there are at least $n$ primes between the $(n+1)$th prime and the product of the first $n+1$ primes. Our proof is based on an elementary counting method (enumerative arguments) and the application of Stirling's formula to give upper bound for some binomial coefficients.

literatureSources.title: Two-dimensional magnetic interactions in LaFeAsO
literatureSources.summary: Inelastic neutron scattering measurements demonstrate that the magnetic interactions in antiferromagnetic LaFeAsO are two-dimensional. Spin wave velocities within the Fe layer and the magnitude of the spin gap are similar to the \textit{A}Fe$_2$As$_2$ based materials. However, the ratio of interlayer and intralayer exchange is found to be less than $\sim 10^{-4}$ in LaFeAsO, very similar to the cuprates, and $\sim$ 100 times smaller than that found in \textit{A}Fe$_2$As$_2$ compounds. The results suggest that the effective dimensionality of the magnetic system is highly variable in the parent compounds of the iron arsenides and weak 3-D interactions may limit the maximum attainable superconducting $T_{c}$.

literatureSources.title: Twin Primes In Quadratic Arithmetic Progressions
literatureSources.summary: A recent heuristic argument based on basic concepts in spectral analysis showed that the twin prime conjecture and a few other related primes counting problems are valid. A rigorous version of the spectral method, and a proof for the existence of infinitely many quadratic twin primes $n^{2}+1$ and $n^{2}+3$, $n \geq 1$, are proposed in this note.

literatureSources.title: Infinitely Many Primes (Using Topology)
literatureSources.summary: Problem: Prove there are infinitely many prime numbers. Solution: First recall that an arithmetic progression with difference $ d$ is a sequence of integers $ a_n \subset \mathbb{Z}$ so that for every pair $ a_k, a_{k+1}$ the difference $ a_{k+1} – a_k = d$. We proceed be defining a topology on the set of integers by defining a basis $ B$ of unbounded (in both directions) arithmetic progressions.

whatWeKnow: Finite computation checked exactly \[ 1\le n\le 200,\qquad n^2+1\le 40001. \] It found \(34\) prime-producing \(n\)’s. A skeptic check confirmed no missing or extra reported prime-producing \(n\)’s in that range.
If \(n\) is odd and \(n>1\), then \[ n^2+1\equiv 2\pmod 4, \] so \(n^2+1\) is composite.
Thus only \(n=1\) and even \(n\) can produce primes.
Equivalently, all nontrivial cases reduce to \[ n=2m,\qquad n^2+1=4m^2+1. \]

For any odd prime \(p\mid n^2+1\), \[ n^2\equiv -1\pmod p, \] so \(-1\) is a quadratic residue modulo \(p\), forcing \[ p\equiv 1\pmod 4. \] This matches the observed small divisors \(5,13,17,29,37,41,\dots\).
Source-backed literature status from the saved run: no supplied source established an unconditional proof that infinitely many primes are of the form \(n^2+1\).
roadblocks: The finite search up to \(n=200\) is evidence only; it proves no infinite claim.
No sieve bound strong enough to isolate infinitely many prime values of \(n^2+1\) has been established in the workspace.
No analytic theorem on the distribution of primes represented by \(n^2+1\) has been proved here.
Multivariable results such as Friedlander–Iwaniec \(X^2+Y^4\) and Merikoski \(X^2+(Y^2+1)^2\) were already rejected as direct routes: they do not control the fixed one-variable slice \(n^2+1\).
The claims that this is “Landau’s fourth problem,” that it is open, Bateman–Horn asymptotics for \(n^2+1\), and weaker almost-prime literature results are currently unsupported by supplied sources.
